passages.passage_text:
We speak of other people's pains, hopes, and suspicions as though they were as available to us as the weather. Yet the grammar of such talk conceals an asymmetry. Of my own pain I need no evidence; of yours I have only what you do and say. The classical problem of other minds begins from this asymmetry and asks what entitles me to believe that behind your behavior there is anything it is like to be you.

The oldest answer is the argument from analogy. I observe that in my own case certain bodily states, such as a burn on the hand, are regularly joined to a certain inner state and to outward behavior such as wincing and withdrawal. When I see another body wince and withdraw from a flame, I reason that the same sort of cause probably produces the same sort of effect. The inference is modest, resting on a single case, namely myself. A generalization from one instance is ordinarily worthless: if I had met only one kind of bird and it happened to be blue, I would not conclude that birds are blue. Defenders reply that the analogy is not offered as a rigorous induction but as the best explanation open to a creature who has only one inner life to consult.

A second response abandons the inference altogether. Writers inspired by Wittgenstein argue that the problem arises from a picture of the mind as a private theatre, to which each of us has sole access and about which language must therefore be a kind of code that no one else can check. But words like "pain" are learned in public, through shared practices of comforting, complaining, and treating wounds. If the meaning of "pain" were fixed by a private sensation that no one else could inspect, no child could ever be taught the word, and no one could be corrected in its use. On this view, behavior is not mere evidence from which an inner state is inferred; it is partly constitutive of what the concept means. Skeptics find this too cheap, since it seems to define the problem away. A person may, after all, feign pain flawlessly, and the possibility of fakery shows that the outward and the inward can come apart.

A third approach, more recent, treats our knowledge of others as a matter of practical skill rather than theory. Developmental studies suggest that infants respond to gaze and facial expression long before they could possibly construct an analogy. We do not first see a body and then deduce a mind; we see a face that is angry, and the anger is as directly perceived as its color. The skeptic's demand for proof assumes that we begin with mere bodies and must climb toward minds, whereas ordinary experience seems to begin with persons.

None of these replies is wholly satisfying, and it is worth asking why the problem persists. Perhaps it is because each answer addresses a different worry. The analogical argument addresses the worry about justification; the linguistic one addresses meaning; the perceptual one addresses the psychology of how we in fact proceed. A thoroughgoing skeptic can grant all three and still ask the original question, whether there is some further fact about your experience that I could never verify. To that question there may be no answer, but it does not follow that the question is idle. It is the shadow cast by the fact that consciousness, unlike a stone, exists from a point of view, and a point of view is precisely what cannot be handed across.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central claim of the passage?

options.A: The argument from analogy is the strongest reply to the problem because it rests on the one case we know best
options.B: The problem of other minds is a pseudo-problem produced by a mistaken picture of the mind as a private theatre
options.C: Developmental research on infants has shown that minds are perceived directly, so the skeptic's demand is misplaced
options.D: Three replies to the problem of other minds address different worries, and none ends the skeptic's questioning

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage surveys analogy, public language, and direct perception, assigns each a distinct target, and ends by saying a skeptic can grant all three and still ask the original question. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage presents analogy as modest and open to the one-case objection, not as the strongest reply. B) Only the Wittgensteinian approach diagnoses a mistaken picture, and the author notes skeptics find it too cheap; the author does not endorse it as dissolving the problem. C) The infant studies support only the third approach, and the author says it merely changes the question.
questions.trap: Choosing the reply the passage describes most vividly as if the author endorsed it, instead of the survey-and-limits structure.

questions.stem: The example of someone who has met only one kind of bird, which happened to be blue, is used by the author to illustrate

options.A: why direct perception of mental states is usually mistaken by observers
options.B: how a private sensation can fix the meaning of a word like "blue" for a speaker
options.C: the way a defender of analogy would support a modest conclusion about other minds
options.D: why an inference drawn from a single instance is usually unreliable

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the bird case is offered as a parallel to the critics' complaint that the argument from analogy generalizes from one case, namely oneself. Why the others are wrong: A) The bird example concerns inference from one case, not perception. B) The example is not about word meaning; the private-meaning point belongs to the Wittgensteinian paragraph. C) The example is the critics' illustration of a weakness, not the defenders' support; defenders reply separately.
questions.trap: Mistaking the critics' illustration of a weakness for part of the defenders' reply.

questions.stem: Proponents of the second response would most likely agree with which of the following claims?

options.A: Behavior is merely a reliable sign of an inner state, which each person must nonetheless infer from a single case
options.B: A word such as "pain" could not be taught or corrected if its meaning were fixed only by a sensation no one else can inspect
options.C: A person who can feign pain flawlessly shows that the concept of pain has no connection to behavior whatsoever
options.D: The meaning of "pain" is learned by comparing a child's private sensations with those reported by other children

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the passage says that if meaning were fixed privately no child could be taught the word and no one corrected, which is the core of this response. Why the others are wrong: A) Treating behavior as mere evidence is the analogical view, which the second response rejects by making behavior partly constitutive. C) Feigning is the skeptic's objection to this view, not a claim its proponents make. D) Comparing private sensations is exactly the private-theatre picture the response denies, since no one can inspect another's sensation.
questions.trap: Attributing the skeptic's objection, or the analogical view, to the Wittgensteinian side.

questions.stem: The author's mention of feigned pain serves chiefly to

options.A: demonstrate that infants cannot perceive anger in a face until they can reason by analogy
options.B: show that the argument from analogy is more reliable than the appeal to public language
options.C: support the skeptic's complaint that outward behavior and inner states can come apart entirely
options.D: establish that no one has ever been deceived about the pain of another person in practice

questions.explanation: Correct: C) feigning is raised as a reason to doubt that behavior is constitutive of pain, since a person may act pained without being so. Why the others are wrong: A) The infant research is in a separate paragraph and is not connected to feigning. B) Feigning is raised against the linguistic view, and no comparison of reliability with analogy is made. D) The point is that deception is possible, so the claim of no deception is the opposite of the author's point.
questions.trap: Reading the example as supporting the paragraph's own view rather than the skeptic's reply to it.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings, if true, would most weaken the third approach?

options.A: Infants respond to a caregiver's smile by smiling before they can speak or walk
options.B: Adults who are shown photographs of faces can reliably label the emotions expressed in them
options.C: Infants show no differential response to faces until well after the age at which they can reason analogically
options.D: Adults sometimes fail to detect a feigned expression of anger displayed by an actor

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the third approach relies on infants responding to gaze and expression before they could construct an analogy; if the response came only after analogical reasoning, that claim would be undercut. Why the others are wrong: A) Early smiling in response to a smile would support the approach. B) Reliable adult labeling is compatible with, and mildly supportive of, direct perception. D) The approach concerns how we ordinarily perceive others, and occasional misperception does not defeat it.
questions.trap: Choosing the answer that mentions fallibility, which does not bear on whether infants respond before analogical reasoning.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the problem of other minds persists mainly because

options.A: the three replies contradict one another, so that accepting one of them requires rejecting the other two
options.B: a skeptic can accept each reply and still ask whether there is a further fact about another's experience that could never be verified
options.C: philosophers have not yet collected enough developmental evidence to decide between rival accounts of how we perceive minds
options.D: the argument from analogy has never been defended against the objection that it generalizes from a single case

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the final paragraph says the replies address different worries and a thoroughgoing skeptic can grant all three while still asking the original question. Why the others are wrong: A) The author describes the replies as addressing different worries, not as contradicting one another. C) The passage does not say that more evidence would settle the matter; the remaining question is about verification in principle. D) Defenders do reply to the single-case objection in the second paragraph.
questions.trap: Treating the persistence of the problem as an empirical gap rather than a point about perspective.

passages.passage_text:
For much of the twentieth century, the dispute over the early Industrial Revolution was a dispute about the standard of living. Optimists, drawing on the aggregate figures for British output, held that mechanization raised the incomes of ordinary workers and that suffering was transitional. Pessimists, drawing on the testimony of contemporaries and on the grim conditions of the new factory towns, held that workers were made poorer, or at least more miserable, by the transition. For decades the quarrel seemed stalemated, because each side was using a different kind of evidence and neither could answer the other's objections.

The stalemate began to give way when economic historians reconstructed price and wage series for the period. The task is harder than it sounds. Wages in the late eighteenth century were rarely reported in a uniform way: a weaver might be paid by the piece, a farm laborer partly in kind, a factory hand by the week with deductions for fines. Historians therefore had to assemble thousands of scattered payrolls and then convert nominal earnings into real earnings by dividing by an index of the cost of a representative basket of goods. The choice of basket matters enormously. A basket weighted toward bread will show one trend when grain prices fall, and another if rents and fuel in crowded towns are rising faster. Different baskets, built in good faith, produced different conclusions.

The most influential revision holds that real wages for much of the working population stagnated for several decades after output began to grow, a delay sometimes called the "Engels' pause" after the observer who described the squalor of Manchester. During those years output per worker rose, yet the gains accrued chiefly to owners of capital in the form of profits. Only after about 1830 did real wages begin a sustained climb. This finding is not a vindication of the pessimists in every respect. It concedes that growth eventually reached ordinary workers, and it leaves open why the lag occurred. Some scholars point to the slow diffusion of the new technologies, which at first employed a small fraction of the labor force. Others stress the pressure of a rapidly growing population, which kept labor cheap. Still others emphasize the bargaining weakness of workers who were legally barred from combining.

A further complication is that wages are not welfare. Urban workers may have earned more than rural ones while breathing worse air, living in smaller rooms, and dying younger. Studies of the heights of army recruits, a rough proxy for childhood nutrition and disease, suggest that the average stature of Britons actually fell for cohorts born in the early decades of industrialization, even as their cash incomes were not falling. One reading is that cash conceals costs borne outside the market. Another is that the migrants to town were selected differently from those who stayed behind, so that comparisons across places mislead.

What the debate teaches, then, is less a verdict than a method. To say that industrialization raised or lowered living standards requires saying for whom, over what interval, and by what measure. The optimists were right that the long-run trajectory was upward and the pessimists were right that the path was neither smooth nor evenly shared. It is possible to hold both positions only if one is willing to let the time horizon do the reconciling, and that is precisely where the historian's choice of horizon becomes as consequential as any statistic.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the optimist-pessimist dispute went unresolved for decades primarily because

options.A: the two camps relied on different kinds of evidence
options.B: contemporary testimony about factory towns was almost entirely unavailable to historians
options.C: aggregate output figures for Britain were too unreliable to support any conclusion about incomes
options.D: neither side was willing to concede that mechanization had affected ordinary workers at all

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the first paragraph says each side used a different kind of evidence and neither could answer the other's objections. Why the others are wrong: B) The pessimists are described as drawing on contemporary testimony, so it was available. C) The passage does not call the output figures unreliable; it says they are a different kind of evidence from testimony. D) Both sides are described as addressing the effect on workers, with optimists claiming gains and pessimists losses.
questions.trap: Blaming missing or defective data when the passage blames mismatched kinds of evidence.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why does the choice of a basket of goods matter when computing real wages?

options.A: A basket weighted toward bread removes the effect of deductions and fines from the nominal earnings of factory workers
options.B: A basket built in good faith always overstates real wages because it omits the goods that workers produced themselves
options.C: A basket is required to convert payment in kind into piece rates before payrolls from different regions can be combined
options.D: Baskets weighted toward different goods can show rising or falling real wages depending on whether grain or rents and fuel changed more

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the author says a bread-heavy basket shows one trend when grain falls and another if rents and fuel in towns rise faster. Why the others are wrong: A) Fines and deductions concern how wages were paid, not how the basket is weighted. B) The passage says baskets built in good faith give different conclusions, not that they systematically overstate. C) The passage does not describe converting payment in kind into piece rates; the basket is used to convert nominal to real earnings.
questions.trap: Confusing problems of reporting wages with problems of pricing a basket.

questions.stem: The "Engels' pause" refers to a period in which

options.A: output per worker rose while the real wages of many workers stayed flat
options.B: real wages rose sharply while output per worker was falling in new factory towns
options.C: industrial output stagnated because workers were legally barred from combining
options.D: profits fell as the new technologies spread to a small fraction of the labor force

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage defines the pause as decades of stagnant real wages after output began to grow, with gains going to capital. Why the others are wrong: B) This reverses the relationship described. C) Output grew during the pause; the bargaining weakness is offered as one explanation for stagnant wages, not stagnant output. D) Profits rose, since gains accrued chiefly to owners of capital.
questions.trap: Reversing the direction of output and wages.

questions.stem: The author cites the heights of army recruits primarily in order to

options.A: show that cash income may fail to capture changes in well-being
options.B: prove that real wages fell for every cohort born after the start of industrialization
options.C: demonstrate that migrants to towns were selected differently from those who stayed behind
options.D: argue that the pessimists were correct about the long-run trajectory of living standards

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the paragraph opens by saying wages are not welfare, and recruits' falling heights are offered as evidence of costs that cash incomes conceal. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says cash incomes were not falling, so height does not prove falling wages. C) Selective migration is offered as one alternative reading, not what the height data demonstrate. D) The author says the optimists were right about the long run.
questions.trap: Treating a proxy for nutrition as direct evidence about wages.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most strongly support the reading that selective migration, rather than hidden urban costs, explains the shorter recruits?

options.A: Town-born recruits were shorter than recruits who migrated to the same towns from the countryside as teenagers
options.B: Recruits from rural districts with falling grain prices were shorter than recruits from districts with rising grain prices
options.C: Men who moved to towns were already shorter, on average, than the men who stayed in the countryside before they moved
options.D: Recruits who worked in factories were shorter than recruits who worked in the same towns as shopkeepers or clerks

questions.explanation: Correct: C) if migrants were already shorter before moving, differences between town and country would reflect who moved, not what towns did to them. Why the others are wrong: A) This would suggest town conditions during childhood mattered, favoring hidden costs. B) This compares districts by grain prices and does not bear on who migrated. D) This compares occupations within towns and does not test selection of migrants.
questions.trap: Selecting evidence that shows a difference in height without showing why it arose.

questions.stem: The author would most likely agree that the statement "industrialization raised living standards" is

options.A: false, because the gains of mechanization accrued chiefly to owners of capital
options.B: true, because real wages eventually began a sustained climb after about 1830
options.C: defensible only if one says for whom, over what interval, and by what measure
options.D: meaningless, because wages and welfare cannot be compared across periods

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the final paragraph says the debate teaches a method of specifying who, when, and by what measure. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says growth eventually reached ordinary workers, so the claim is not simply false. B) The author treats the long-run upward trend as real but warns against ignoring the path and its distribution. D) The author compares wages and welfare, concluding they differ, not that comparison is meaningless.
questions.trap: Taking a single piece of evidence as a verdict when the author says the lesson is methodological.

passages.passage_text:
Readers raised on print tend to imagine that a poem, once composed, exists as a fixed text, and that any variation between two tellings of it is a corruption. The study of living oral epic overturned this assumption in the twentieth century. Fieldworkers who recorded singers of tales in the mountain villages of the Balkans found that a bard might perform the "same" song on different evenings at very different lengths, and that he would insist, sincerely, that the songs were identical. The singer's idea of sameness was not ours. For him the song was the story, its characters and sequence of incidents, not a particular string of words.

What made such performance possible was a stock of formulas, metrically fitted phrases for recurring ideas: the dawn, the hero's arrival, a ship setting out. Formulas, in the influential account of the scholars who studied these singers, were not clichés but a technology. A poet composing aloud, before an audience, in strict meter, cannot pause to hunt for the right word. He draws from a reservoir of units that he has absorbed over years of apprenticeship, and he combines them according to inherited patterns. Typical scenes, such as the arming of a warrior or the assembling of a council, supply larger building blocks. On this theory, the epic was composed in performance, and the Homeric epics, with their recurring epithets, were the end product of such a tradition committed at some moment to writing.

The theory has been enormously fertile, but it has also drawn objections. Some critics note that formulaic diction is found in much written verse, so that its presence proves nothing about oral composition. Others observe that the Balkan evidence, collected in the twentieth century from singers who often lived beside literate neighbors, may not represent a pre-literate world. Still others argue that the model underestimates artistry. If the singer merely recombines inherited material, how are we to account for the effects of surprise, irony, and structure that readers have long admired? Defenders answer that the tradition's constraints are not a cage but a grammar. A fluent speaker is not less creative because he uses words he did not invent.

A different line of work asks what such epics are for. In societies without writing, a song of the deeds of ancestors is a repository of collective memory: genealogies, claims to land, models of conduct. Performance is therefore a social event in which the audience shapes the telling, calling for a favorite episode or showing impatience, and the singer adjusts. The poem has no single author because it has many custodians. Writing, when it arrives, does not simply preserve this poem; it changes what a poem is. A text can be consulted, compared, and criticized in a way that a performance cannot. The very notion of a "correct" version, and the corresponding notion of a corrupted one, may be an artifact of the page.

If this is right, the modern reader who pores over a printed epic is in an odd position. He holds, frozen, the trace of an art whose essential feature was that it was never frozen. To read it well may require a kind of imaginative reconstruction, hearing in the repeated epithets not repetition but the pulse of a voice that had to keep going.

questions.stem: When a Balkan bard insisted that two quite different performances were "identical," he most likely meant that

options.A: the metrical formulas were drawn from the same stock of phrases, in the same order and number
options.B: the performances had been memorized from a single fixed text taught to him by an earlier singer
options.C: the audience had approved each telling to the same degree and had requested the same episodes
options.D: the characters and the sequence of incidents were the same, whatever the wording or length

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the first paragraph says the song was the story, its characters and incidents, not a particular string of words. Why the others are wrong: A) Formulas are described as a compositional device, and the singer's sameness is not about them; the lengths and words differed. B) This is the print-bound notion of sameness that the passage says the singer did not share. C) Audience reaction is discussed later as shaping a telling, not as defining sameness.
questions.trap: Importing the print-culture idea of a fixed text into the singer's own view.

questions.stem: According to the formulaic theory, the primary function of formulas is to

options.A: signal to the audience that a poem is very ancient
options.B: preserve the exact wording of a poem across generations
options.C: allow a poet to compose fluently in meter while performing
options.D: make a poem easier for later scribes to transcribe accurately

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the passage calls formulas a technology for a poet who cannot pause to hunt for words while composing aloud in strict meter. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage does not connect formulas to signaling age. B) Exact preservation of wording is the print assumption the passage contests; versions vary. D) Transcription is mentioned only as a later event.
questions.trap: Assuming that repeated phrases exist to fix a text in memory.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the objection that formulaic diction does not prove oral composition?

options.A: Balkan singers who could read performed songs with fewer recurring epithets than singers who could not read
options.B: Several oral performances of the same story by one singer differ in length by a factor of two or more
options.C: Formulas in a recorded epic are used more frequently in battle scenes than in scenes of council or travel
options.D: A long poem composed in writing by a known author contains many metrically fitted recurring epithets

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the objection is that formulaic style occurs in written verse; a documented written poem with formulas is a direct instance. Why the others are wrong: A) This would suggest literacy changes style, which fits the oral theory better than the objection. B) Variation in length is the observation the oral theory uses, not evidence against it. C) The distribution of formulas across scene types does not bear on whether composition was oral.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about oral performance when the objection concerns written verse.

questions.stem: The comparison to a fluent speaker who uses words he did not invent is offered in order to argue that

options.A: working within inherited conventions need not prevent a poet from producing original and artful effects
options.B: a singer who recombines inherited material cannot be credited with any artistry in the telling of a song
options.C: a poet's use of familiar phrases is evidence that the poet was unable to read or write at all
options.D: the vocabulary of an oral tradition is as large as that of any speaker of the same language

questions.explanation: Correct: A) defenders say constraints are a grammar, and a speaker is not less creative for using inherited words. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the critics' worry that the analogy answers. C) Literacy is not at issue in the analogy. D) The analogy concerns creativity and constraint, not the size of a vocabulary.
questions.trap: Reversing the defenders' point into the critics' objection.

questions.stem: The author suggests that the notion of a "corrupted" version of an epic

options.A: arose among the singers who learned their songs from literate teachers
options.B: may be a product of writing rather than of the tradition itself
options.C: first appeared when audiences began to request particular favorite episodes
options.D: is necessary for understanding why singers vary their songs

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the fourth paragraph says that correct and corrupted versions may be an artifact of the page. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage ties the notion to writing, not to the singers' teachers. C) Audience requests are part of how performance varies and do not originate the idea of corruption. D) The passage says the notion is an artifact, not a necessity for understanding variation.
questions.trap: Misplacing the source of the corruption idea in performance rather than in the text.

questions.stem: The final paragraph most strongly suggests that a reader of a printed epic should

options.A: discard the repeated epithets as later additions made by scribes
options.B: treat the printed version as the correct text against which others are corrupted
options.C: try to recover imaginatively the sound and urgency of a performance
options.D: regard the epic as the work of one author whose intentions can be recovered

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the author says reading well may require imaginative reconstruction, hearing the pulse of a voice that had to keep going. Why the others are wrong: A) The epithets are treated as meaningful traces of performance, not scribal additions. B) This adopts the page-bound notion the passage questions. D) The passage says the poem has many custodians rather than a single author.
questions.trap: Slipping back to the print-based assumptions the passage has been challenging.

passages.passage_text:
Monuments are usually thought of as instruments of remembrance, but the history of public commemoration suggests they are just as often instruments of forgetting. A statue of a general on a plinth tells the passer-by what to admire and relieves him of the need to think further. The traditional memorial, with its heroic figure, its inscribed names of the fallen, and its elevated position above the crowd, assumes that memory is a settled matter, that the community already knows what happened and what it means. Such monuments were built to consolidate victories and legitimate regimes, and they performed that function efficiently.

In the late twentieth century, a different kind of memorial began to appear, especially in countries confronting episodes of which they were not proud. Its designers rejected the vertical and the triumphant. One celebrated example in Washington is a polished black wall sunk into the ground, with names cut into its surface in the order of death rather than in alphabetical order or by rank. Visitors descend toward it and see their own reflections among the names. The design offers no narrative and no verdict on the war it commemorates; its critics at first denounced it as a gash, a monument to shame, and demanded that a conventional statue be added nearby. A statue was added, yet it is the wall that people touch, and on which they leave letters and photographs.

Architectural theorists have called such works counter-monuments, and they argue that they respond to a distinctive problem. After mass atrocity, any monument that claims to resolve the past risks offering the public a comfortable closure. In Berlin, one memorial to the murdered Jews of Europe consists of a field of concrete slabs of varying height on an undulating ground. There is no center, no inscription at the entrance, and no single route. Visitors lose their bearings and sight of one another. The designer has insisted that the work is not meant to explain anything. Some praise this refusal as honest; others find it evasive, observing that a space which says nothing may be filled by whatever meaning the visitor brings, including indifference. The photographs of tourists posing on the slabs have been cited as evidence of the danger.

The dispute turns on a question about what memory is. If remembering is the transmission of a fixed lesson, then ambiguity is a failure. If it is an activity that must be performed anew by each generation, then a monument should provoke rather than conclude. The second view has the further merit of acknowledging that communities are divided about their past; a design that imposes one reading will be contested, defaced, or toppled, as recent controversies over statues of colonial and slaveholding figures have shown. A monument that invites interpretation cannot be refuted, only continued.

Yet the second view is not without costs. Memory that is left wholly open to the visitor may drift toward the sentimental, and a space that asks to be experienced may be experienced as mere atmosphere. The most successful memorials may be those that pair an open form with modest, factual information, trusting stone to move and text to anchor. Between the monument that dictates and the monument that merely suggests lies a narrow path, and public memory, like the buildings that hold it, depends on how well it is walked.

questions.stem: The first paragraph characterizes the traditional memorial as one that

options.A: treats the meaning of the past as already settled and asks the viewer to accept it
options.B: invites each generation of visitors to arrive at its own interpretation of events
options.C: was designed chiefly to console families of the fallen rather than to praise leaders
options.D: avoids narrative so that the community remains free to disagree about its past

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the author says the traditional memorial assumes memory is settled and tells passers-by what to admire. Why the others are wrong: B) This describes the counter-monument. C) The passage says traditional monuments consolidated victories and legitimated regimes. D) Avoiding narrative is the counter-monument's strategy.
questions.trap: Attributing the counter-monument's features to the traditional form.

questions.stem: The detail that the names on the black wall are ordered by date of death most plausibly indicates that the designers wished to

options.A: make individual names easier for visitors to locate on the wall
options.B: honor officers before enlisted soldiers in the order of their service
options.C: avoid implying a hierarchy or a settled story among the dead
options.D: reproduce the layout used on traditional memorials of earlier wars

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the contrast with alphabetical order or rank, together with the absence of a narrative or verdict, suggests a refusal of hierarchy. Why the others are wrong: A) Alphabetical order would be easier to search, and the author contrasts the design with it. B) Rank is explicitly listed as what the order avoids. D) The author presents the design as a departure from the traditional memorial.
questions.trap: Choosing a practical rationale when the passage frames the design in terms of meaning.

questions.stem: The author's reference to photographs of tourists posing on the slabs is meant to illustrate which risk of an open design?

options.A: A memorial with no inscription may be misread by visitors as a purely decorative public sculpture
options.B: A memorial that disorients visitors may cause them to avoid the site and the history it commemorates
options.C: A memorial built on uneven ground may endanger visitors who cannot see where they are walking
options.D: A space that explains nothing may be filled with whatever meaning visitors bring, including indifference

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage explicitly links the photographs to the danger that an unexplained space invites indifference. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage does not discuss visitors misreading the work as decoration; the concern is indifference. B) The passage says visitors lose their bearings but does not say they avoid the site. C) Physical safety is never raised.
questions.trap: Choosing a plausible practical risk the passage never mentions.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the claim that a monument imposing a single reading will be contested?

options.A: Monuments built by regimes that later lost power were often removed after the regime fell
options.B: Monuments to a widely shared national experience stood without dispute for centuries
options.C: Monuments to contested wars drew more protest than monuments to peaceful achievements
options.D: Visitors left more objects at open memorials than at conventional statues

questions.explanation: Correct: B) if statues with a single reading stayed uncontested across generations, the claim that they will be contested would be weakened. Why the others are wrong: A) Removal after a regime falls supports contest of imposed readings. C) More protest of contested wars is consistent with the claim. D) Objects left at open memorials concern visitors' response to the open form, not whether single readings are contested.
questions.trap: Selecting evidence consistent with, rather than opposed to, the claim.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the phrase "cannot be refuted, only continued" most nearly means that an open monument

options.A: has been proven by critics to be more accurate than a conventional statue
options.B: will be defended by the public against every attempt to remove or alter it
options.C: makes no claim that could be refuted, so viewers can extend its meaning
options.D: must be completed by additions of text before its message becomes clear

questions.explanation: Correct: C) a work that offers no single reading makes no assertion to refute, and each generation adds to its interpretation. Why the others are wrong: A) No claim of accuracy is made. B) The passage says nothing about public defense of open monuments against alteration. D) The author warns that text should anchor, but does not say a message depends on it.
questions.trap: Reading the phrase literally rather than as a point about interpretation.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's final position on open and directive memorials?

options.A: Open memorials are clearly superior to directive ones because they allow every visitor to find a private meaning
options.B: Neither type is fully adequate, and a memorial combining an open form with brief factual information may serve best
options.C: Directive memorials should be restored because open memorials have encouraged indifference among their visitors
options.D: The choice between the two types is purely aesthetic and does not affect how a community remembers

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the last paragraph names costs of the open view and proposes pairing open form with modest factual text. Why the others are wrong: A) The author lists costs of the open view and so does not call it clearly superior. C) The author does not call for restoring directive memorials, which are said to be contested. D) The author states that public memory depends on how the path between the two is walked.
questions.trap: Choosing an extreme position when the passage ends on a middle path.

passages.passage_text:
When the American folk revival reached its height in the early 1960s, its audiences were largely urban, young, and college-educated, and what they prized in the music was its supposed purity. A ballad collected from an Appalachian farmer was valued precisely because it had not been made for money. The revivalists spoke of "the real thing" and distrusted anything that smacked of show business. The irony, noticed even at the time, was that the rural singers whom collectors celebrated often had no such scruples. Many had learned songs from phonograph records and radio broadcasts, performed for pay at county fairs, and would happily sing a popular tune if the listener preferred it.

The notion of authenticity at work here deserves scrutiny, for it combines two ideas that are not obviously compatible. One is that authentic music is old, transmitted orally from generation to generation without the intervention of commerce. The other is that authentic music is sincere, the honest expression of a performer's own experience. A singer born in a city who learns a coal-mining ballad from a library recording might sing it with complete sincerity and yet fail the first test. A rural performer who sings a song by rote, indifferent to its words, might pass the first test and fail the second. Revival audiences moved between the criteria without noticing the shift.

Scholars sometimes describe authenticity not as a property of the music but as a judgment made about it, a social agreement about what counts as genuine. On this view, the judgment reveals the anxieties of those who make it. Listeners in a postwar society of suburbs and mass production were drawn to an imagined community of the rural poor because it appeared to stand outside commerce. Their enthusiasm may have done real good, since the revival brought attention, recordings, and income to aging musicians who had been forgotten. But it also froze them in a role. A performer who adopted a new style, or plugged in an amplifier, was accused of betrayal, as happened to one famous songwriter at a festival in 1965, when some in the crowd responded to his electric set with jeers.

It would be easy to conclude that authenticity is simply a fiction, and many cultural critics have. But that conclusion is too quick. Fictions can be productive. The belief that a song carries the weight of a particular place and history led young musicians to study that history and to learn the techniques of the older players with a care they might not otherwise have given. Moreover, the demand for sincerity, whatever its philosophical difficulties, serves as a check on cynicism: an audience that cares whether a performer means what she sings is an audience that will notice when she does not.

The most defensible position may be a modest one. Authenticity cannot be a fixed quality of a repertoire, for repertoires have always been mixed, borrowed, and sold. It might instead be understood as a relation between performer, material, and audience, one that must be earned in each performance, and that can fail even when every historical credential is in order.

questions.stem: The "irony" noted in the first paragraph is that

options.A: the rural singers prized by collectors often did not share the revivalists' distaste for commerce
options.B: the revivalists were unable to find any rural singers willing to perform old ballads
options.C: college-educated audiences preferred popular recordings to the ballads of Appalachian farmers
options.D: county fairs paid rural performers less than urban concert halls paid revival singers

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the author contrasts the revivalists' distrust of show business with rural singers who learned from records and performed for pay. Why the others are wrong: B) The passage says collectors did find and celebrate such singers. C) Audiences are said to have prized the music's purity. D) No comparison of pay is made.
questions.trap: Missing that the irony concerns the performers' attitudes, not the audiences' tastes.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a city-born singer who sincerely performs a coal-mining ballad learned from a library recording

options.A: meets the standard of sincerity but not the standard of oral transmission without commerce
options.B: meets the standard of oral transmission without commerce but not the standard of sincerity
options.C: fails both standards because a performer must share the experience the song describes
options.D: meets both standards because sincerity is enough to make a performance authentic

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage says such a singer could be fully sincere yet fail the first test, namely old oral transmission outside commerce. Why the others are wrong: B) This reverses the two standards; it describes the rural singer who sings by rote. C) The passage says sincerity is an honest expression of the performer's own experience and does not require sharing the song's setting. D) The passage says the singer would fail the first test.
questions.trap: Swapping which of the two authenticity tests the singer passes.

questions.stem: The view that authenticity is a social judgment rather than a property of the music is most consistent with which observation?

options.A: Every ballad collected from a rural farmer is judged authentic by every listener
options.B: A performance becomes more authentic whenever the singer's voice is recorded accurately
options.C: Two audiences can hear the same performance and disagree about whether it is genuine
options.D: Authentic songs can be distinguished from imitations by examining their melodies alone

questions.explanation: Correct: C) if authenticity were a judgment, different groups could judge one performance differently. Why the others are wrong: A) Universal agreement would suggest an objective property. B) Recording quality is unrelated to the judgment described. D) Examining melodies alone treats authenticity as a property of the music.
questions.trap: Assuming that agreement among listeners proves a property of the object.

questions.stem: The author mentions the jeers at the 1965 festival chiefly as an example of how the revival

options.A: confined performers to the role of preserving an older style, and treated change as betrayal
options.B: gave aging musicians the income and the attention they had long been denied by record companies
options.C: encouraged young musicians to study the history of the songs they chose to perform in public
options.D: showed that audiences cared whether a performer meant what he sang, as the author later argues

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage says the revival froze performers in a role, and the electric set drew accusations of betrayal. Why the others are wrong: B) This is a benefit the author notes, but not what the festival example illustrates. C) This is the productive-fiction point from the next paragraph. D) The jeers concern style change, not the sincerity point.
questions.trap: Choosing a point the passage makes elsewhere instead of the one the example supports.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the claim that authenticity is merely a fiction is best described as

options.A: enthusiastic agreement, because the revival rested on a mistaken ideal
options.B: complete rejection, because authenticity is a fixed property of old repertoires
options.C: studied neutrality, because the evidence cannot decide the question
options.D: qualified resistance, since fictions can have useful effects

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the author calls the conclusion too quick and then lists productive effects of the belief. Why the others are wrong: A) The author does not agree that the idea is merely a fiction. B) The author says repertoires have always been mixed, so authenticity is not fixed. C) The author argues a position, namely a modest relational view.
questions.trap: Reading a qualified view as either full agreement or full rejection.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most weaken the claim that belief in authenticity motivated careful study of older players?

options.A: Young revival musicians who valued authenticity visited older players more often than they visited other performers
options.B: Older players were invited to festivals in larger numbers after the revival began than before
options.C: Audiences at revival concerts paid higher ticket prices than audiences at other kinds of concerts
options.D: Young revival musicians who valued authenticity studied older recordings no more than those who did not

questions.explanation: Correct: D) if valuing authenticity did not predict more study, the proposed motivational effect would be undermined. Why the others are wrong: A) More visits would support the claim. B) Invitations to festivals concern income and attention for older players, not the motivation of younger ones. C) Ticket prices say nothing about the study of older techniques.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact about the revival that is related in topic but not in logic.

passages.passage_text:
In the twentieth century, planners came to regard the street as a problem of circulation. Wide avenues, separated land uses, and towers set back in parks all reflected the conviction that a city worked best when people and vehicles moved efficiently between homes, workplaces, and shops. The critics who answered this view, most famously a journalist who lived in a crowded neighborhood of lower Manhattan, argued that it mistook the purpose of the street. A sidewalk, she wrote, was not merely a corridor but a place where strangers learned to live together, and its safety derived not from police but from the casual vigilance of shopkeepers, residents, and passersby who had reasons to be there at different hours.

Sociologists have given this intuition several names, among them "eyes on the street" and "civil inattention." The latter, a term associated with the sociologist Erving Goffman, describes a courteous convention in which strangers acknowledge one another's presence and then look away, granting each other privacy in public. Such habits are easy to overlook because they work. They make possible a form of sociability that is neither intimate nor hostile, which urbanists have regarded as a distinctive achievement of city life: the capacity to be among people unlike oneself without needing to know them.

Yet public space has never been equally open to all. Historians of the nineteenth-century city note that respectable women, the poor, and racial minorities were frequently made to feel unwelcome in precisely those squares and promenades that were celebrated as common ground. Today the exclusions are subtler. Benches designed with armrests to prevent lying down, spikes on ledges, and rules against loitering do not forbid anyone by name, yet they tell certain people to move on. Privately owned plazas, created by developers in exchange for permission to build taller towers, are open to the public in name but are policed by guards who decide what conduct is acceptable. A space that looks public may not be a place in which the public has rights.

Such developments have prompted a debate between two ideals. One treats public space as a stage for democratic life: a place where citizens may assemble, protest, and encounter dissent. The other treats it as an amenity: a clean, comfortable, well-managed space in which people may rest and consume. The two ideals are compatible up to a point, since a pleasant plaza draws a crowd. But they diverge when management begins to define comfort as the absence of anything unsettling. Many urban parks have been revitalized by conservancies that raise private money and impose strict standards of order, and the results can be admirable by any measure of cleanliness and safety. Whether they are also admirable as democratic spaces is less clear.

There is no reason to think the question can be answered in general. The street that supports casual contact among strangers in one neighborhood may be a site of harassment in another, and a plaza that welcomes protest in one decade may be fenced in the next. What can be said is that public space is not a given but an achievement, continually renegotiated, whose character depends on who is permitted to linger and who is moved along. To ask what a city's public spaces are like is therefore to ask, indirectly, who the city thinks its public is.

questions.stem: The critics of mid-century planning, as described in the first paragraph, held that planners had mistaken

options.A: a source of public revenue for a mechanism that could be used to raise private investment
options.B: a place for commercial exchange for an arena in which political disagreement is settled
options.C: a site of potential crime for a system that police officers could easily supervise
options.D: a setting for the social life of strangers for a channel for moving people efficiently

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the critics argued the sidewalk is a place where strangers learn to live together, not merely a corridor for circulation. Why the others are wrong: A) Revenue and investment are not discussed in the critique. B) The critics' point concerns circulation, not commerce or politics. C) The critics said safety derives from casual vigilance rather than police.
questions.trap: Choosing a contrast that sounds like urban planning but ignores the circulation-versus-sociability point.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations best exemplifies "civil inattention"?

options.A: Two neighbors on a sidewalk stop to chat about their families for several minutes
options.B: A shopkeeper notices a stranger loitering and calls the police to report him
options.C: A commuter stares at a fellow passenger to learn what he is reading
options.D: Two strangers on a crowded train glance at each other briefly and then each turns to a book

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the term describes acknowledging a stranger's presence and then looking away, granting privacy. Why the others are wrong: A) A conversation between neighbors is a form of acquaintance, not civil inattention. B) Reporting a stranger is vigilance or policing rather than courteous privacy. C) Staring is the opposite of looking away.
questions.trap: Confusing civil inattention with the vigilance of the 'eyes on the street' idea.

questions.stem: The armrests on benches and spikes on ledges are mentioned as examples of

options.A: exclusion that works through design rather than through rules naming particular groups
options.B: measures that planners adopted to encourage casual contact among strangers
options.C: practices that were common in nineteenth-century squares but that no longer occur
options.D: ways in which private developers have paid for the public use of plazas

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the author says they do not forbid anyone by name yet tell certain people to move on. Why the others are wrong: B) They are described as discouraging some people, not encouraging contact. C) The passage says today's exclusions are subtler, not that these devices are historical. D) Plaza bargaining with developers is a separate example.
questions.trap: Confusing the examples of design-based exclusion with the privately owned plaza.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the two ideals of public space diverge when

options.A: managers come to treat the absence of anything unsettling as the definition of a comfortable space
options.B: citizens begin to assemble in plazas in numbers that exceed the capacity that designers anticipated
options.C: conservancies raise private money that governments would otherwise have spent on parks and benches
options.D: protest becomes more frequent in a district than the casual contact among strangers that preceded it

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage says the ideals diverge when management defines comfort as the absence of anything unsettling. Why the others are wrong: B) Crowd size is not discussed as the point of divergence. C) Private funding is described as producing admirable results in cleanliness and safety, not as the divergence. D) The passage does not compare frequencies of protest and casual contact.
questions.trap: Selecting an increase in activity when the divergence is about managerial definitions.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would most support the suggestion that conservancy-managed parks may be less democratic than unmanaged ones?

options.A: Conservancy parks are cleaner and have fewer reported crimes than nearby unmanaged parks
options.B: Conservancies ban political gatherings that are permitted in nearby parks without private management
options.C: Conservancies raise most of their funds from donors who live near the parks they support
options.D: Visitors to conservancy parks report greater satisfaction with benches and lawns

questions.explanation: Correct: B) a ban on assembly or protest that is absent in unmanaged parks bears directly on the democratic ideal. Why the others are wrong: A) Cleanliness and safety are the admirable results the author already grants. C) Donor residence says nothing about access or assembly. D) Satisfaction reflects the amenity ideal.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about amenity quality when the question concerns democratic function.

questions.stem: The final sentence of the passage implies that a city's public spaces

options.A: are determined by the laws governing private ownership of plazas
options.B: can be evaluated by the single standard of cleanliness and safety
options.C: reveal whom the city regards as belonging to its public
options.D: have the same social function in every neighborhood and decade

questions.explanation: Correct: C) asking about the character of public spaces is said to ask who the city thinks its public is. Why the others are wrong: A) Private ownership is one example, not the determinant of everything. B) The passage says cleanliness is not the whole measure of democratic value. D) The author says the function varies across neighborhoods and decades.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing one example as the author's general claim.

passages.passage_text:
A public good, in the economist's definition, has two features: it is non-excludable, in that no one can be prevented from enjoying it once it exists, and non-rival, in that one person's enjoyment does not diminish another's. National defense, clean air, and a lighthouse are the standard examples. Because no one can be made to pay, each person has an incentive to let others bear the cost; this is the free-rider problem, and it is the usual explanation for why markets underprovide such goods and why governments tax citizens to supply them.

The argument has an air of inevitability that has been questioned from several directions. The first challenge is empirical. In laboratory experiments in which participants decide how much of an endowment to contribute to a common pool, the pattern of contributions is not what the simple theory predicts. Subjects contribute substantial amounts at first, though less than would be socially optimal, and contributions decay over repeated rounds as people notice that others are contributing less. Contributions rebound if participants are given the option to punish non-contributors, even at a cost to themselves. The finding suggests that many people are conditional cooperators, willing to contribute if others do, and that the free rider is not the whole story but one type among several.

A second challenge is historical. The lighthouse, a textbook example of a good that private enterprise cannot supply, was in fact supplied privately along parts of the English coast for centuries. Shipowners paid fees collected at the port, and the lighthouse owners held patents from the Crown. The case shows that excludability can be engineered, by linking a payment to some other service the user cannot do without. It does not follow that every public good can be handled this way, and the example is sometimes used to prove more than it can. Many lights, after all, were built only because the Crown granted a legal monopoly, which is a form of state action.

A third challenge comes from studies of communities that manage shared resources, such as irrigation systems and fisheries, without either privatization or central control. The political scientist Elinor Ostrom documented that such communities often succeed when they have clear boundaries of membership, rules suited to local conditions, inexpensive means of monitoring, and graduated sanctions for violators. Her work is usually classified under common-pool resources rather than pure public goods, since these resources are rival. Still, it showed that the choice between market and state is not exhaustive.

None of this refutes the free-rider analysis. The analysis remains a sound account of what happens when large anonymous groups must cooperate without any means of enforcement. What the challenges show is that the standard conclusion, that a good of this kind will be underprovided without government coercion, rests on assumptions about human motivation and about institutions that are not always met. The theory is best read not as a prediction but as a statement of a problem that societies have solved in many different ways, some through taxation, some through custom, and some through arrangements that no theorist had imagined in advance.

questions.stem: The decay of contributions over repeated rounds in the laboratory experiments is best explained, according to the passage, by the fact that

options.A: every participant is a free rider who contributes only until the endowment is exhausted
options.B: participants learn that punishing non-contributors costs more than the benefit it brings
options.C: many participants are conditional cooperators who give less as others give less
options.D: the common pool is non-rival, so each added contribution lowers the value of the others

questions.explanation: Correct: C) the author says subjects contribute at first and then reduce giving as they notice others contributing less, which fits conditional cooperation. Why the others are wrong: A) If all were free riders, initial contributions would be near zero, and the passage says they were substantial. B) The passage says contributions rebound when punishment is available, so punishing is not described as futile. D) Non-rivalry is a property of the good, and does not explain a decay pattern.
questions.trap: Using the pure free-rider model to explain data the passage says it fails to predict.

questions.stem: The author says that the lighthouse example is sometimes used "to prove more than it can" because

options.A: private lighthouses were supplied only along parts of the English coast and never anywhere else in Europe
options.B: shipowners refused to pay fees at ports unless the lighthouse owners held patents from a private guild
options.C: lighthouse fees were collected so rarely that owners depended on voluntary donations to keep the lights burning
options.D: many privately owned lights depended on a legal monopoly granted by the Crown, a form of state action

questions.explanation: Correct: D) the passage says many lights were built only because the Crown granted a monopoly, so private provision was not independent of the state. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says only 'parts of the English coast' and makes no claim about the rest of Europe. B) The patents came from the Crown, not a private guild, and fees were collected. C) Fees were paid by shipowners at ports; voluntary donations are not mentioned.
questions.trap: Choosing a fact that sounds like a limit but that the passage does not state.

questions.stem: The author notes that Ostrom's work concerns common-pool resources, which are rival, in order to

options.A: suggest that irrigation systems and fisheries are better managed by governments than by communities
options.B: caution that her findings do not directly refute the analysis of pure public goods
options.C: argue that rival goods are always provided more efficiently by markets than by the state
options.D: explain why the communities she studied lacked clear boundaries of membership

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the author says her results show the market-versus-state choice is not exhaustive but classifies the resources as rival, limiting the inference. Why the others are wrong: A) Ostrom's work shows communities managing resources themselves. C) The passage says the choice between market and state is not exhaustive. D) Clear boundaries are listed as a condition of success.
questions.trap: Overextending a counterexample from rival resources to all public goods.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would the author most likely view as consistent with the free-rider analysis?

options.A: Contributions to a common pool rose in small groups of strangers after participants were allowed to punish non-contributors
options.B: Contributions to a common pool fell toward zero in large anonymous groups that had no means of punishment or enforcement
options.C: A fishing village kept its catch sustainable by using local rules, inexpensive monitoring, and graduated sanctions
options.D: A private company collected fees from every ship passing a coast by tying payment to a mandatory harbor service

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the author says the analysis remains sound for large anonymous groups without enforcement. Why the others are wrong: A) Rising contributions under punishment are one of the findings the passage uses to challenge the simple theory. C) Village management without state or market is the third challenge to the standard conclusion. D) Linking payment to another service shows excludability can be engineered, a challenge to the standard conclusion.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that supports the challenges rather than the analysis the author says still stands.

questions.stem: A town's volunteer flood-warning system is staffed reliably because members know one another and notice when someone skips a shift. This arrangement most closely resembles

options.A: a lighthouse that is funded through port fees
options.B: a community with inexpensive monitoring and graduated sanctions
options.C: an experiment in which subjects contribute anonymously
options.D: a government service paid for through taxation

questions.explanation: Correct: B) mutual knowledge and noticing absences correspond to the monitoring and sanction conditions Ostrom documented. Why the others are wrong: A) Port fees are a fee-linking arrangement, not community monitoring. C) Anonymity is absent in the town's system. D) Taxation involves state coercion, which the volunteer system does not.
questions.trap: Matching the example to the first familiar solution rather than to the one with the same mechanism.

questions.stem: The final paragraph suggests that the free-rider theory is best understood as

options.A: a refuted hypothesis that is no longer useful for understanding cooperation
options.B: a statement of a problem that societies solve in varied ways
options.C: an exact forecast of how large anonymous groups will behave in every setting
options.D: a justification for replacing market provision of goods with state provision

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the author says the theory is best read as a statement of a problem with many solutions. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says none of the challenges refutes the analysis. C) The author says the standard conclusion rests on assumptions not always met, so it is not an exact forecast everywhere. D) The author says solutions include custom and other arrangements besides taxation.
questions.trap: Reading the author's limits on the theory as a rejection of it.

passages.passage_text:
Discussions of public trust in science often begin from what is called the deficit model: the assumption that distrust arises from ignorance, so that the remedy is to supply the public with more facts. The model has an obvious appeal for scientists, who tend to believe that anyone who understood the evidence would reach the same conclusion. But decades of research on controversies from nuclear power to vaccination have found that knowledge and trust are only weakly related. People who know a good deal about a technology may be more worried than those who know little, and attempts to correct beliefs by repeating facts sometimes fail to move them at all.

An alternative approach starts from the observation that trust is not primarily a matter of evaluating claims. Nobody can personally verify more than a minuscule fraction of the scientific findings on which modern life depends. Ordinary people, like ordinary scientists, rely on testimony, and the relevant question becomes whom to believe. Philosophers who have analyzed this problem argue that trust is reasonable when it tracks trustworthiness, and that trustworthiness has several components: competence, honesty, and a concern for the interests of those who rely on the expert. A public that doubts a scientific institution may be doubting not its competence but its motives, particularly if the institution has a history of concealing risks or has been aligned with commercial interests.

History supplies ample reason for such doubt. Episodes in which authorities reassured the public and were later proved wrong, whether about medical treatments, environmental contamination, or the safety of food, leave a long memory. Communities that were the subjects of unethical research, such as the men who were observed but not treated for syphilis in a famous American study, have understandable grounds for suspicion, and the suspicion may be passed on to people who never took part. Distrust of this kind is not irrational. It is a response to evidence, though the evidence concerns institutions rather than the natural world.

None of this implies that all opinions are equally well grounded. Some skepticism is manufactured. Documented campaigns by industries have sought to create the appearance of scientific doubt about the hazards of their products, deliberately emphasizing uncertainty that the research community did not share. The existence of such campaigns complicates the argument above, since it shows that doubt can be cultivated for advantage and that it is not always a sign of an honest response to a past betrayal. Telling the two apart is difficult for a layperson, and it is a task for which no simple rule exists.

What follows for scientists is uncomfortable. It is not enough to be right; they must also be seen to be trustworthy, and that may mean admitting uncertainty openly, disclosing financial ties, and listening to communities rather than lecturing them. Some will regard such steps as a concession to unreason. But if trust is a relationship rather than a verdict on a set of claims, the maintenance of the relationship is part of the scientific enterprise, not a public-relations afterthought.

questions.stem: The deficit model, as described in the passage, assumes that

options.A: public distrust of science results from a lack of knowledge
options.B: scientists distrust the public because it cannot evaluate evidence
options.C: knowledge of a technology reliably increases worry about its risks
options.D: distrust arises mainly from the commercial alignment of institutions

questions.explanation: Correct: A) the passage defines it as the assumption that distrust arises from ignorance, so supplying facts is the remedy. Why the others are wrong: B) The model concerns the public's distrust of science, not the reverse. C) The passage reports that knowledgeable people may be more worried, which is a finding against the model, not part of it. D) This is part of the alternative approach.
questions.trap: Attributing the alternative approach's explanation to the deficit model.

questions.stem: Which finding described in the passage most directly challenges the deficit model?

options.A: Communities that were subjects of unethical research may pass their suspicion on to people who never took part
options.B: Industries have run documented campaigns to create an appearance of scientific doubt about the hazards of their products
options.C: Few ordinary people can personally verify more than a minuscule fraction of the scientific findings they rely on
options.D: People who know a good deal about a technology may be more worried about it than people who know little

questions.explanation: Correct: D) if knowledge and trust are weakly related, or inversely related, supplying facts will not reliably produce trust. Why the others are wrong: A) This supports the institutional-history explanation but does not address whether knowledge raises trust. B) Manufactured doubt complicates the alternative account and does not test the deficit model directly. C) This supports the testimony argument, not a test of knowledge against trust.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that supports the alternative view without bearing on the deficit assumption.

questions.stem: The author regards distrust among communities that were subjects of unethical research as

options.A: an irrational reaction that scientists can correct by disclosing more facts
options.B: a reasonable response to evidence about how institutions have behaved
options.C: a form of manufactured doubt created by industries seeking commercial advantage
options.D: a consequence of ignorance about the competence of research scientists

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the author says this distrust is not irrational, being a response to evidence about institutions. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says it is not irrational and that facts alone may not address it. C) Manufactured doubt is a separate category, and the author says no such mechanism is claimed here. D) The author says such doubt concerns motives and history more than competence.
questions.trap: Equating all distrust with either ignorance or manipulation.

questions.stem: The author mentions industry campaigns to manufacture doubt in order to

options.A: prove that every expression of public skepticism about science has been deliberately produced by commercial interests
options.B: qualify the claim that distrust reflects honest responses to past betrayals, since some doubt is cultivated for advantage
options.C: argue that scientists should avoid disclosing financial ties so that campaigns cannot exploit them
options.D: show that the philosophical account of trust as tracking trustworthiness has been refuted by the evidence

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the author says the campaigns complicate the earlier argument by showing doubt can be cultivated and is not always honest. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says some skepticism is manufactured, not all. C) The author recommends disclosure, not avoiding it. D) The author says the argument is complicated, not refuted.
questions.trap: Overextending a qualification into a sweeping claim.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most support the claim that trust tracks perceived trustworthiness rather than knowledge?

options.A: Public trust in an institution rose after a campaign that repeated its findings, with the same reported conflicts of interest
options.B: Public trust in an institution was lower among citizens who had read more of its published reports
options.C: Public trust in an institution rose after it disclosed its financial ties, with public knowledge of the facts unchanged
options.D: Public trust in an institution did not differ between citizens who owned shares in industry and citizens who did not

questions.explanation: Correct: C) a rise in trust after disclosure, with facts held constant, points to trustworthiness as the operative factor. Why the others are wrong: A) A rise after repeating findings would fit the deficit model. B) Lower trust among those with more knowledge challenges the deficit model but does not isolate trustworthiness as the cause. D) Shareholding does not test either factor.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that is merely against the deficit model rather than for the trustworthiness account.

questions.stem: The phrase "not a public-relations afterthought" in the last sentence suggests that maintaining trust is

options.A: a task that scientists should delegate to professional communicators
options.B: part of the scientific enterprise itself rather than a secondary task
options.C: unnecessary when the scientific evidence on a question is strong
options.D: a concession to unreason that scientists should make only reluctantly

questions.explanation: Correct: B) the author says that if trust is a relationship, maintaining it is part of the enterprise. Why the others are wrong: A) The author places the responsibility on scientists, not on communicators. C) The author says it is not enough to be right. D) The author reports that some scientists regard it as a concession to unreason but disagrees.
questions.trap: Adopting the objection the author reports as if it were the author's own view.

passages.passage_text:
In the nineteenth century, John Henry Newman defended the university as a place devoted to the cultivation of the intellect for its own sake. Knowledge, he argued, is its own end, and a liberal education forms habits of judgment that outlast any particular subject. Around the same time, in the German states, a rival conception was emerging: the research university, in which the professor was not merely a teacher but an investigator, and students were initiated into the production of new knowledge. The modern university is a hybrid of these two, and like many hybrids it is prone to internal tension.

The tension is most visible in debates about the value of what universities do. Governments and families increasingly ask what a degree is for, and the answers they expect are economic: higher earnings, employability, contributions to innovation. Universities have responded by publicizing their role in the economy, in some cases by creating offices to license patents and attract industrial partners. Such activities can be defended as extending the benefits of research to society. But they raise a worry that the university's distinctive value, the disinterested pursuit of understanding, will be crowded out by what can be measured and sold. Fields that cannot promise a return, such as the study of ancient languages, are first to feel pressure.

Defenders of the economic emphasis reply that the older ideal was always an idealization. Newman's university served the sons of a narrow elite for whom the leisure to pursue knowledge for its own sake was a privilege, and the research university's ties to state and industry date back to its origins in the training of officials and the support of national projects. To insist on purity, they say, is to forget who was excluded. Expanding access to higher education has required justifying it to taxpayers in terms they understand.

There is another consideration that tends to fall between the two camps. The usefulness of knowledge is notoriously hard to predict. Mathematical results once thought to be curiosities have later become the foundation of cryptography; studies of the behavior of bacteria in unusual environments have yielded tools of molecular biology. If the practical payoff of inquiry is often unforeseeable, then a university that organized itself strictly around foreseeable returns would be worse at producing useful results, not better. On this argument, the case for unfettered inquiry can be made on utilitarian grounds, which may be more persuasive to a skeptical public than an appeal to the intrinsic dignity of the mind.

The argument has a limit, though. It justifies freedom of inquiry as a means, and what is justified only as a means may be abandoned when a better means appears. A university that defends itself solely by its eventual usefulness has conceded the premise of its critics, namely that its worth is to be measured by its outputs. Newman's insistence that knowledge is an end is therefore not merely nostalgic; it names a commitment that cannot be derived from any calculation of benefit, and without which the calculation itself would lose its point.
